morphology.summary: An organelle, not a cell: a polarised stack of smooth, flattened, disc-shaped membrane sacs (cisternae) sitting in the cytosol next to the nucleus, with vesicles arriving on one face and budding off the other. It is the cell's sorting, glycosylation and packaging station on the secretory route from the endoplasmic reticulum to the plasma membrane, lysosomes and secretory granules.
morphology.kind: membrane-bound organelle of eukaryotic cells (absent from bacteria and archaea)
morphology.size: Each cisterna is a flattened disc roughly 0.5-1 um across (cell-type dependent). The luminal gap in the flat central plate is very narrow, about 10-20 nm, while the rims are dilated to roughly 40-60 nm. A whole stack of 4-8 cisternae is therefore only about 0.3-0.5 um thick and 1 um wide - about the footprint of a single bacterium. Fenestrae (membrane-bounded holes), mostly near the rims, are up to ~100 nm across.
morphology.shape: A stack of curved, parallel, flattened saccules lying on top of one another like a pile of slightly warped pita breads or a stack of deflated pancakes. The cisternae are smooth-surfaced and usually curved, giving the stack a shallow bowl or crescent profile in section. Each cisterna is thin and flat in the middle and swells (dilates) at its edges; the dilated rims are perforated by fenestrae and drawn out into tubules, and vesicles bud from them. The last one or two trans cisternae are markedly more tubular/reticulated and appear to be peeling off the stack.
morphology.number_per_cell: A typical mammalian cell contains roughly 40-100 stacks (dictyosomes). In vertebrate cells these stacks are joined laterally by tubular bridges into a single continuous perinuclear 'Golgi ribbon', so it reads as one organelle. Plant cells instead keep hundreds of separate, dispersed dictyosomes. A teaching image should show ONE stack (optionally with a hint of a neighbouring stack connected by a lateral tubule).
morphology.position_in_cell: Perinuclear and juxtanuclear: in animal cells the ribbon sits beside the nucleus, wrapped around the centrosome, held there by microtubules and the minus-end motor dynein. The cis face looks toward the nucleus and the transitional/rough endoplasmic reticulum; the trans face looks outward toward the plasma membrane. Rough ER cisternae (ribosome-studded, in contrast to the smooth Golgi) typically lie just beyond the cis face.
morphology.polarity: Strongly polarised, structurally, biochemically and functionally. Cis (entry, 'forming', cis-Golgi network) face = convex, receives COPII-derived carriers from ER exit sites via the ERGIC / vesicular-tubular clusters. Then medial cisternae. Then trans (exit, 'maturing', trans-Golgi network) face = concave, buds secretory vesicles, lysosome-bound carriers and clathrin-coated vesicles. Cisternae also grow subtly thicker/denser and more electron-dense from cis to trans, and glycosylation enzymes are distributed in a cis-to-trans gradient. This cis/trans asymmetry is the single most important thing an illustration must get right.
morphology.appearance_in_tem: In thin-section TEM the stack appears as a set of 4-8 dark, closely apposed parallel lines (the paired membranes of each flattened cisterna) with a barely visible lumen between them, bowed into a shallow arc; the ends of the lines swell into rounded profiles, and the surrounding cytoplasm on the concave/trans side is crowded with small round vesicle profiles. The membranes are smooth - completely free of the black ribosome dots that stud the neighbouring rough ER.
morphology.colour_note: The Golgi is colourless in life; TEM images are greyscale. All colour in a teaching illustration is convention. Use a cis-to-trans colour gradient to make the polarity obvious at a glance.

structures.note: The whole pile of 4-8 flattened cisternae, curved into a shallow bowl. This is the body of the organelle and should dominate the picture.
One disc-shaped sac: thin and flat in the middle, swollen at the rim, smooth-surfaced. 0.5-1 um across, lumen only 10-20 nm in the centre. Draw 4-8 of them, clearly separate, never fused.
The narrow enclosed space inside each sac where cargo is glycosylated. Show it as a thin bright slit between the two membrane leaflets, widening at the rims.
The convex receiving side, turned toward the nucleus and the ER. Incoming vesicles arrive here. In a labelled drawing this face must be visibly convex and visibly different from the trans face.
A tubular, perforated, net-like first compartment lying against the cis face, where arriving carriers fuse. Draw as a lacy tubular fringe on the convex side, not as a clean flat plate.
The two to four middle sacs between cis and trans, the main glycosylation workshop. Flattest and most regular of the stack; the classic 'parallel lines' in a micrograph.
The concave shipping side, turned away from the nucleus toward the plasma membrane. Vesicles bud off here. Its cisternae are more dilated, more irregular and more fragmented than the cis ones.

The last one or two trans cisternae, heavily reticulated and tubular and appearing to peel away from the stack. The main sorting station: cargo leaves here for the cell surface, for lysosomes or into secretory granules.
Each flat sac balloons out at its edges. This bulge is where cargo concentrates and where vesicles bud. A stack drawn with uniformly thin, straight-edged sacs looks wrong.
Membrane-bounded holes up to ~100 nm wide, concentrated near the rims. In a face-on or cutaway view they read as small round perforations in the disc; in section they read as gaps in the line.
Thin membrane tubules streaming sideways from the cisternal rims; in vertebrates they bridge neighbouring stacks into the Golgi ribbon. Draw as a few fine tendrils leaving the edges of the stack.

structures.en: COPII transport vesicle arriving from the ER
structures.note: Small (~60-80 nm) coated vesicles budded at ER exit sites, approaching the cis face. Show a few on the convex side, some with a faint coat, moving toward the Golgi.

A loose cloud of fused vesicles and short tubules sitting between the ER exit site and the cis face - the staging area. Draw as a small irregular grape-like cluster of interconnected vesicles and tubules, not as a neat sac.

structures.en: COPI vesicle (retrograde recycling, Golgi-to-ER and intra-Golgi)
structures.note: Small coated vesicles budding at the rims and travelling backwards, cis-ward. Useful for showing that traffic is two-way; a couple with a small arrow is enough.

structures.en: Secretory vesicle budding from the trans face
structures.note: Larger, cargo-filled vesicles pinching off the TGN on the concave side and heading for the plasma membrane. Show at least one caught mid-budding, still attached by a neck.
Optional detail at the trans face: a vesicle with a bristly polyhedral coat, the route to lysosomes via mannose-6-phosphate receptors.

structures.en: Rough endoplasmic reticulum (context, beyond the cis face)
structures.de: Raues endoplasmatisches Retikulum (Umgebung, jenseits der cis-Seite)
structures.note: Context only, at the edge of the frame on the cis side. This is the one structure that IS studded with ribosomes - the contrast with the smooth Golgi is the teaching point.
Optional context at the frame edge to establish which way is 'in'. Never draw the Golgi itself as a nucleus.
The granular ground substance the organelle floats in, with free ribosomes scattered in it (free, NOT attached to the Golgi membranes).

structures.en: Golgi ribbon (neighbouring stack linked by tubules)
structures.note: Optional: a partial second stack at the edge of the frame joined to the first by lateral tubules, to show that the mammalian Golgi is a ribbon of linked stacks.

do_not_draw: Do NOT stud the cisternae with ribosomes. The Golgi is a SMOOTH-membraned organelle; ribosome-studded sacs are rough endoplasmic reticulum. Ribosomes may appear free in the cytosol or on a nearby rough ER cisterna used as context, never on the Golgi membranes themselves.
Do NOT draw cristae. Inward folds of an inner membrane belong to a mitochondrion. Golgi cisternae are separate, closed, flattened sacs, not shelves projecting into a common matrix.
Do NOT fuse the stack into one continuous tube, snake or coiled ribbon of a single lumen. The cisternae are discrete compartments; cargo does not flow through a single pipe.

Do NOT draw a symmetric, featureless stack with no cis/trans distinction. Both faces looking identical is the classic textbook-cartoon error. The cis face must be convex and receiving, the trans face concave, more dilated, more fragmented and shedding vesicles.
Do NOT draw it as a nucleus with a double envelope and nuclear pores. No pore complexes, no nucleolus, no chromatin.

Do NOT draw a bacterial cell: no cell wall, no peptidoglycan, no capsule, no nucleoid, no plasmid, no flagellum, no pili, no fimbriae. The Golgi is an organelle inside a eukaryotic cell and prokaryotes do not have one.
Do NOT draw a plasma membrane closing around the Golgi as if it were a cell. It has no boundary of its own beyond its cisternal membranes; it sits loose in the cytosol.
Do NOT give it a nucleoid, DNA, ribosome factories or any genome of its own. Unlike mitochondria and chloroplasts, the Golgi has no DNA and no double outer membrane.
Do NOT draw the sacs as uniformly thin flat plates with straight cut edges. The rims must be visibly dilated and fenestrated, with tubules and budding vesicles at the edges.
Do NOT draw the cisternae as a stack of thick, plump, sausage-like tubes or a pile of doughnuts. They are very thin flattened discs (lumen 10-20 nm in the centre against a 0.5-1 um diameter).
Do NOT draw thylakoid grana. Stacked green discs inside a chloroplast look superficially similar and are a common confusion; the Golgi has no pigment, no stroma and no surrounding envelope.
Do NOT draw stacked ER cisternae or annulate lamellae instead: those are parallel sheets without cis/trans polarity, without dilated fenestrated rims and without a vesicle cloud at one face.
Do NOT draw it as a lysosome or a secretory granule: no single large round electron-dense body, no dense core, no hydrolase-filled sphere.

Do NOT reverse the polarity: vesicles must ARRIVE on the convex cis side (from the ER, nucleus-ward) and DEPART from the concave trans side (toward the plasma membrane). Arrows pointing the wrong way are a hard fail.
Do NOT draw more than about 8-9 cisternae in one stack (4-8 is the mammalian norm), and do not draw fewer than 4.
Do NOT anthropomorphise it: no face, no eyes, no limbs. No text, letters, numbers, scale bars, arrows-with-labels or watermarks baked into the image.

colour_legend.golgi_stack: the whole stack carries a continuous cis-to-trans gradient from #F2B441 amber through #E3765E terracotta to #5C6CC4 indigo
colour_legend.cisterna: each sac takes the gradient colour of its level in the stack; membrane outline one shade darker than its fill
colour_legend.cis_golgi_network: #F2B441 (warm amber - the receiving end; warmest colour of the gradient)
colour_legend.medial_cisternae: #E3765E (terracotta / coral, shifting through the middle of the stack)
colour_legend.trans_golgi_network: #5C6CC4 (indigo-blue - the shipping end; coolest colour of the gradient)
colour_legend.cisternal_lumen: #FFF6E6 (pale cream, the narrow bright interior slit)
colour_legend.dilated_rims: same hue as the parent cisterna, one shade deeper and more saturated
colour_legend.fenestrations: #FFFFFF (openings read as holes of background colour through the disc)
colour_legend.copii_transport_vesicle: #7FC8A9 (mint green, with a faint stippled coat)
colour_legend.ergic: #5FA88C (deeper sea-green cluster of fused vesicles and tubules)
colour_legend.copi_retrograde_vesicle: #C9A227 (mustard, distinct from the mint COPII vesicles)
colour_legend.secretory_vesicle: #4F86C6 (clear blue, matching the trans end it buds from)
colour_legend.clathrin_coated_vesicle: #3E5C8A (dark slate blue with a bristly polyhedral rim)
colour_legend.rough_er: #9AA7B5 (cool grey-blue sheets with dark ribosome dots)
colour_legend.nucleus_context: #6E7B8B (muted slate, softly out of focus at the frame edge)
colour_legend.cytosol: #EDE7DC (warm neutral pale grey-beige ground with fine granularity)
colour_legend.golgi_ribbon: desaturated echo of the main stack's gradient, ~40% opacity, at the frame edge
colour_legend.note: The Golgi has no colour in life and TEM is greyscale; every colour here is teaching convention. The point of the palette is the cis-to-trans gradient - warm amber/orange at the convex receiving face running through terracotta to violet/indigo at the concave shipping face - so the polarity is legible without reading a single label.

sources.title: Alberts et al., Molecular Biology of the Cell, 4th ed. - 'Transport from the ER through the Golgi Apparatus' (NCBI Bookshelf NBK26941)
sources.note: Canonical textbook account: stacks of four to six cisternae (up to 60 in some flagellates), cis and trans faces each served by a network (CGN / TGN), vesicular tubular clusters between ER and Golgi, ribbon near the nucleus and centrosome in animal cells versus hundreds of dispersed dictyosomes in plants.

sources.title: Cooper, The Cell: A Molecular Approach, 2nd ed. - 'The Golgi Apparatus' (NCBI Bookshelf NBK9838)
sources.note: States explicitly that the cis face is convex and usually oriented toward the nucleus and the trans face concave, and lays out the four functional regions (CGN, medial, trans, TGN) and the ER-Golgi intermediate compartment.

sources.title: Madame Curie Bioscience Database - 'The Golgi Apparatus' (NCBI Bookshelf NBK6268)
sources.note: Source for the dimensional detail: cisternal diameter 0.5-1 um (cell-type dependent), narrow central lumen 10-20 nm, dilated rims perforated by fenestrae up to ~100 nm, 3-11 cisternae per stack, rims extended into tubules and tubular networks, membranes smooth from lack of ribosomes.

sources.title: Klumperman, 'Architecture of the Mammalian Golgi', Cold Spring Harbor Perspectives in Biology 3:a005181 (2011)
sources.note: Peer-reviewed review of Golgi ultrastructure: polarised cis-to-trans stack, cisternal number robustly conserved per cell line, electron-tomography reconstructions, lateral tubular bridges linking stacks into the ribbon, TGN peeling off the trans side.

sources.title: Appenzeller-Herzog & Hauri, 'The ER-Golgi intermediate compartment (ERGIC): in search of its identity and function', Journal of Cell Science 119:2173 (2006)
sources.note: Reference for the ERGIC / vesicular-tubular cluster: COPII carriers bud at ER exit sites and fuse into an interconnected vesicular-tubular compartment (marker ERGIC-53) between the ER and the first cis cisterna, with COPI budding retrogradely from it.

sources.title: Martinez-Alonso, Tomas & Martinez-Menarguez, 'Morpho-functional architecture of the Golgi complex of neuroendocrine cells', Frontiers in Endocrinology 4:41 (2013)
sources.note: Describes the Golgi ribbon as adjacent stacks separated by non-compact regions containing tubules and vesicles, with CGN and TGN at either end - the basis for the peripheral tubular network label.

sources.title: Wikipedia - Golgi apparatus
sources.note: Source for the per-cell counts: 40-100 stacks of cisternae in a mammalian cell, four to eight cisternae usually present per stack (up to 60 in some protists), stacks linked into a ribbon near the centrosome, COPII in and COPI recycling.

sources.title: Wikipedia (de) - Golgi-Apparat
sources.note: German terminology check: Golgi-Apparat, Dictyosom, Zisternen, cis-Golgi-Netz (konvex) und trans-Golgi-Netz (konkav), Transportvesikel, sekretorische Vesikel; 40-100 Stapel je Saeugerzelle, 4-8 Zisternen je Stapel.

sources.title: Terminologia Histologica (FIPAT/IFAA) - Preface, and Cruz Gutierrez et al., 'Persistencia de Eponimos en Terminologia Histologica', Int. J. Morphol. 34(4) (2016)
sources.note: Verifies the Latin term: Terminologia Histologica lists the organelle as Complexus golgiensis (code H1.00.01.3.0146), also given as Apparatus golgiensis - one of the handful of eponyms deliberately retained in TH. The official TH Preface (https://ifaa.unifr.ch/Public/EntryPage/PDF/TH%20Preface.pdf) cites 'Complexus Golgiensis' as an example.

sources.title: Derganc, Mironov & Svetina, 'Physical factors that affect the number and size of Golgi cisternae', Traffic 7:85 (2006)
sources.note: Quantitative geometry of a cisterna: flat central plate with a toroidal rim of radius ~26 nm (total rim thickness ~52 nm), rim-to-flat area ratio ~0.08 for a 1 um cisterna - the basis for drawing thin plates with distinctly swollen edges.

sources.title: Ladinsky et al., 'Golgi structure in three dimensions: functional insights from the normal rat kidney cell', J. Cell Biol. 144:1135 (1999)
sources.note: Electron-tomography reconstruction of mammalian Golgi: seven cisternae per stack in the cell types examined, adjacent stacks connected by tubular bridges between cisternae at equivalent levels.

reference_micrograph_candidates.title: Human leukocyte, showing Golgi - TEM
reference_micrograph_candidates.attribution: Louisa Howard, Rippel Electron Microscope Facility, Dartmouth College (via Wikimedia Commons). JEOL 100CX TEM.
reference_micrograph_candidates.note: BEST CANDIDATE. High-magnification thin section of a single human white blood cell in which one Golgi stack fills the lower half of the frame: about six or seven closely apposed dark parallel membrane lines bowed into a shallow crescent, rims visibly dilated into rounded profiles, and a dense cloud of vesicle profiles filling the concave (trans/TGN) side. The concave side faces up-and-inward, the convex cis face down-and-outward, so the cis/trans polarity is directly readable. 640x480, 50 nm scale bar, public domain, uncluttered by other organelles. Verified: HTTP 200, image/jpeg, 99 kB.

reference_micrograph_candidates.title: Golgi apparatus of a human leukocyte with TGN and lateral tubules annotated (derivative of the Dartmouth TEM)
reference_micrograph_candidates.attribution: JeanOhm (Wikimedia Commons), modifications of File:Human leukocyte, showing golgi - TEM.jpg by Louisa Howard (public domain)
reference_micrograph_candidates.note: The same field as candidate 1, cropped and labelled in-image with 'cis face', 'Golgi Stack', 'TGN' and white arrows marking tubules extending laterally from the stack. Excellent as a verification key for the label set - it confirms which face is cis (the convex one, bottom) and where the peripheral tubular network sits - but the burnt-in text makes it unsuitable as a render reference. 649x465, 100 nm scale bar. Verified: HTTP 200, image/jpeg, 121 kB.

reference_micrograph_candidates.title: Golgi in the cytoplasm of a macrophage in the alveolus (lung) - TEM
reference_micrograph_candidates.attribution: Louisa Howard, Rippel Electron Microscope Facility, Dartmouth College (via Wikimedia Commons). JEOL 100CX TEM.
reference_micrograph_candidates.note: Second, independent stack in a mammalian alveolar macrophage, running diagonally across the frame. Shows the dilated, tubulated cisternal rims and the associated vesicle field particularly well, and includes neighbouring organelles for scale. Slightly more cluttered than candidate 1 and the stack is cut more obliquely, so the cis/trans polarity is less obvious. 640x480, 200 nm scale bar. Verified: HTTP 200, image/jpeg, 165 kB.

reference_micrograph_candidates.title: TEM of a cultured hepatocyte showing nucleus, rough ER, Golgi and mitochondria
reference_micrograph_candidates.attribution: Roach DR, Garrett WM, Welch G, Shuboni-Mulligan DD, Caperna TJ, Talbot NC et al., PLoS ONE 10(4): e0123282 (2015), Fig. 3E (cropped); via Wikimedia Commons
reference_micrograph_candidates.note: Context shot rather than a close-up: a whole-cell field with the Golgi (g), rough ER (rer), nucleus (n) and mitochondria (m) all labelled in one frame. Valuable specifically for the do-not-draw checks - it shows side by side that the Golgi membranes are smooth while the neighbouring rough ER is ribosome-studded, and that the mitochondrion with its cristae looks nothing like a Golgi stack. Burnt-in letter labels and a 0.5 um scale bar. 746x570. Verified: HTTP 200, image/png, 401 kB.
